title: pigeonhole — S3 storage that keeps its bytes in chat messages
meta_desc: An educational storage system in Rust: an S3 gateway that cuts objects into chunks and posts them to Telegram and Discord channels, with a metadata log that lives there too.
hero.title: S3 storage that keeps its bytes in chat messages
hero.lede: pigeonhole speaks the S3 API, cuts objects into chunks and posts them as files to Telegram and Discord channels — or to a local disk. Its own metadata is a log of commands, and that log can live in a channel too.
replay.note: A real recording, not an animation drawn by hand: site/record.py ran the pigeonhole binary with JSON logs on and the AWS CLI against it, and this page plays the log back. The two channels are in-memory stores standing in for Telegram and Discord — everything above the store is the same code. The chunk size is lowered to 4 MiB so small files make several chunks (the default is 19 MiB). Played at human speed; the real time is next to each line.
js.say.CreateBucket: Bucket {bucket} created: no upload, one entry in the metadata log.
js.say.PutObject: {key} ({size}) became {chunks}, each posted to both channels; one log entry records the chunks and the object together.
js.say.PutObjectZ: {key} ({size}) became {chunks}: zstd shrank it to {stored} on the wire. Text compresses; random bytes do not.
js.say.CopyObject: {key} is a copy, and nothing was uploaded: the new object points at the same {chunks}, their refcount goes up. Only the log grows.
js.say.ls: The listing comes from memory: the state the log was replayed into. No channel is read.
js.say.end: That's it: two objects' worth of chunks in two channels, and a log that can rebuild everything from scratch.
how.title: How it works
how.sub: Four ideas carry the whole thing.
how.1.d: An object becomes chunks of up to 19 MiB. zstd compresses each 1 MiB block on its own, so a Range read fetches only the blocks it touches.
how.2.d: Each chunk is a file in a channel: posted to every member of a replica group, or to the least loaded shard. A shared limiter paces the calls to Telegram's and Discord's rate limits.
how.3.d: Every S3 operation is one entry in a command log; on boot the state is rebuilt from a snapshot and the log after it. The log can live on disk or in a channel, fenced by message order.
how.4.d: Copies share chunks by refcount. A repair task re-replicates chunks that lost a copy, and a sweeper deletes posts that nothing points to.
feat.title: What it can do
feat.s3.d: Buckets, objects, multipart uploads, Range reads, shallow CopyObject, tagging, user metadata and conditional writes (If-Match, If-None-Match). Works with the AWS CLI, boto3 and rclone.
feat.stores.d: Telegram over MTProto (logged in as a bot), Discord channels, a local disk on segment files, and memory for tests. A Bazel / Buck2 remote cache (REAPI v2) is an optional second gateway.
feat.groups.d: Stores combine into replica groups (every chunk to every member, with a write quorum) and shards (one member per chunk, for throughput). Several bots can share one channel.
feat.log.d: Commands in a fenced log, applied to in-memory state, snapshots in a store of their own, log retention, and a boot that falls back to an older snapshot if the newest is damaged.
feat.heal.d: Background repair and scrub, a sweeper with written-down invariants, uploads pinned before they start, and a crc on every stored block.
feat.raft.d: The tablet runs on openraft. A network that carries Raft messages through chat channels passes 3-node tests — elections, failover, partitions — over a simulated chat; live runs are next.
feat.obs.d: Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboards for stores, the limiter, the log and Raft; structured logs with a span per request, store call and commit.
feat.sim.d: Fault injection in every store, deterministic simulation with madsim, conformance suites per store kind, s3-tests, and CI that caps function complexity.
ontop.title: Real software on top
ontop.sub: S3 with conditional writes is enough for programs that coordinate through S3. They run on a Telegram channel without knowing it.
ontop.etcd.d: An etcd cluster (T4) keeps its state in pigeonhole: elections, transactions, leases, and a leader killed with kill -9 handing over.
ontop.sqlite.d: Litestream streams a SQLite database into pigeonhole; it is deleted, restored, and restored as of a moment in the past.
ontop.cond.d: Conditional writes decided in the log: ten writers race for one key with curl, exactly one wins.
num.title: In numbers
more.title: Coming to this site
more.demos.d: Recorded scenarios to step through: Range reads by block, a channel going dark and repair bringing the copies back, delete and the sweeper, a crash and the log replayed.
more.inside.d: The layers and their traits, how the log is fenced in a channel, and Raft carried by chat messages.
more.built.d: The repository as infographics: growth by layer, the crate graph, where the code lives, and who was at the keyboard.
more.article.d: The story behind it, with this site as the illustrations.
foot.warn: An educational project, not a file host. Using a messenger as general-purpose storage may break the Telegram and Discord terms of service; keep real runs to small test data in a private channel you own.
try.title: pigeonhole, running in your browser
try.lede: Not a recording. The server's Rust code — the metadata tablet on openraft, chunking and zstd, the replica group, the S3 handlers, and the Telegram and Discord stores themselves — is compiled to WebAssembly and runs in a Web Worker on this page. Only the services are fakes: in-memory channels that behave like Telegram and Discord. Nothing leaves your browser.
try.lede_plain: pigeonhole's Rust code compiled to WebAssembly, running in your browser.
try.note: Built from crates/web: the server's crates, read from the same pigeonhole.toml (below). Fake channels stand in for the services (fake = "memory", a build with the fake feature). Times are measured inside the worker.

js.wiz.status: Set up your pigeonhole: nothing runs until you start it.
js.wiz.caption: Pick the channels, the copies, where the metadata lives and how fast the bots may post. The graph on the left follows your choices.
js.wiz.channels_lede: A file is cut into chunks, and each chunk becomes a message: a document, or text if it is small. Pick the channels the node posts them to.
js.wiz.copies_lede: With more copies a chunk survives a lost channel; with fewer, the channels share the work and hold more.
js.wiz.quorum: A write counts once this many copies are posted
js.wiz.quorum_note: {q} of {n}: the rest are posted in the background, and repair fills in a copy that failed.
js.wiz.one_channel: One channel: one copy of each chunk.
js.wiz.all_copies: Every chunk goes to all {n} channels.
js.wiz.all_shards: The {n} channels are shards: each chunk goes to one of them, the least busy.
js.wiz.mixed: {shards} shards of {copies} copies: each chunk goes to one shard, to every channel in it.
js.wiz.meta_lede: The node keeps its metadata (buckets, objects, where each chunk is) as a log of commands, posted to a channel of its own, and snapshots of it.
js.wiz.log_note: Every change is an entry. A restart reads the log back and is where it was.
js.wiz.snapshots_note: The whole state as one file: a restart starts from it and replays only what came after.
js.wiz.every: A snapshot every so many entries
js.wiz.every_note: Fewer entries between snapshots: a faster restart, more snapshot posts.
js.wiz.bots_lede: A bot may post only so often to a channel. More bots on a channel, more posts a minute: each has a budget of its own.
js.wiz.bots_note: The node sends each call through the bot whose budget is ready soonest.
js.wiz.pace: How fast a bot may post
js.wiz.pace_real_note: Telegram lets a bot post about 20 messages a minute to a channel, Discord about 60. Uploads wait for their turn, as on a real server.
js.wiz.pace_demo_note: 20 posts a second per bot: nothing waits, so you see the rest of the system.

js.demo.fault_note: Break it: take the channel down, or clear it as an admin might. Reads go to another copy; a check finds what is gone, and repair puts it back.
js.demo.fault_down_note: The channel is down: every call to it fails. An upload whose write quorum needs this copy fails; with a smaller quorum it counts, and repair adds this copy once the channel is back.

js.say.failed_down: The upload failed: a channel is down, and the write quorum needs its copy. {error}
